Engineered to Win: Scanning, AI, and High-Performance Dentistry

Written by: Todd Snyder, DDS

INTRODUCTION

In racing, speed alone is not enough. Anyone can press the accelerator. But winning requires precision, control, timing, data, and the ability to make the right decision at the right moment.

The same is now true in dentistry. For years, intraoral scanners were viewed as optional digital upgrades—useful and impressive, but not essential. That mindset is changing. In the modern dental office, scanning is no longer just a replacement for impression material. It is becoming a foundational technology that connects diagnosis, treatment planning, patient communication, laboratory collaboration, restorative accuracy, and overall practice performance.

Make no mistake: the race toward the next generation of dentistry has already begun—and the practices that win will be the ones built to compete.

A race car is not simply fast because it has horsepower. It is fast because it is engineered to win. The engine, brakes, tires, suspension, aerodynamics, telemetry, pit crew, and driver all perform as one integrated system. Remove any element—or fail to connect them—and the advantage disappears.

As a cosmetic dentist and professional race car driver, I see a direct relationship between high-performance racing and high-performance dentistry. On the track, the fastest car does not always win—the best-prepared, best-engineered car wins. The driver who understands the machine, trusts the data, hits the apex, manages the braking point, and exits the corner with control is the one who gains the advantage.

Dentistry is entering the same performance era. Today’s progressive practice is no longer simply a place where procedures are performed. It is a system, and every touchpoint affects profitability. How the patient enters, how records are captured, how the condition is diagnosed, how treatment is presented, how the laboratory receives information, and how the final restoration is delivered—each one shapes the patient experience, the clinical outcome, and the performance of the practice.

For the single-chair concierge practice, this is especially valuable. A single-chair office does not win by volume. It wins by excellence, experience, efficiency, and execution. Every interaction must matter. Every piece of technology must earn its place (Figure 1).

Increasingly, artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of that system. AI platforms such as Annie (helloannie.com) can answer phones after hours and support website interactions 24/7, helping ensure patient inquiries are not missed. AI-driven systems can respond to questions, manage online engagement, and help convert interest into scheduled appointments. Pearl AI supports radiographic diagnosis by helping clinicians identify pathology, bone loss, caries, and periapical findings with greater consistency. AI-powered design tools can merge scan data, photography, and CBCT imaging to generate 3D renderings and smile simulations (DTX Studio [Envista]). In a single-chair concierge practice, where there is no large front desk or back-office team, these AI systems become essential members of the crew.

This is where the intraoral scanner plays a pivotal role. A scanner such as the Ori 3.0 Intraoral Scanner (Ori Imaging) becomes part of the performance platform of a modern practice (Figure 2). Its value extends far beyond a digital impression. A single scan can support comprehensive evaluation, diagnostic wax-up, whitening trays, smile design, crown and veneer restorations, orthodontic aligners, surgical guides, laboratory communication, case presentation, and long-term documentation.

In a high-performance single-chair concierge practice, this becomes even more critical. Think of a single-chair office like an F1 car—not designed to carry more people, but to maximize every component, every system, and every second. (Figure 3). There is no room for wasted motion, outdated workflows, or equipment that creates drag. The office must be lean, fast, precise, and deeply connected.

However, technology alone does not create the win. A race car without strategy is just an expensive machine. Without a plan, data interpretation, and trained execution, the race is lost before it begins. Simply purchasing a scanner does not make a practice faster or more profitable. Implementing one with strategy, workflow, training, and a clear clinical purpose is what sets the practice up to win.

The win comes from the engineered system. Speed matters—but speed without precision is chaos. Speed with systems is performance.

CASE REPORT

PATIENT PRESENTATION AND COMPREHENSIVE EVALUATION

A patient presented seeking improvement in the overall appearance of her smile. Her concerns included tooth color, tooth shape, worn incisal edges, uneven contours, and a desire for a more confident, harmonious result (Figures 4 and 5).

As with any aesthetic case, the first step was not to discuss treatment options, but to understand the patient’s desires and complete a comprehensive evaluation. Aesthetic dentistry must begin with conversation, followed by diagnosis. The evaluation included full-face and smile photography (Nikon), retracted intraoral images, radiographs, and CBCT imagery (OP 3D EX [DEXIS]) (Figures 6 and 7), periodontal assessment, occlusal evaluation, existing restoration analysis, and an intraoral digital scan (Figures 8 and 9). AI-assisted radiographic analysis (Pearl AI) supported the diagnostic process by helping identify areas of concern and adding another layer of detection alongside the clinical examination (Figure 10).

The scan captured the patient’s current dentition, arch form, occlusal relationship, restorative space, and existing wear patterns. Next, a 3D facial scan was generated using the Qlone app and aligned with the CBCT image (Figure 11). Combined with CBCT data, the scan allowed AI-powered software (DTX Studio) to generate 3D renderings of the patient’s anatomy, giving both clinician and patient a more complete understanding of the existing condition before treatment was proposed (Figures 12 to 14). This digital record became the foundation for the entire treatment process.

In racing, the driver does not guess where the car is losing time. The team studies speed traces, braking points, tire temperature, lap sectors, and steering input. The data reveals where performance is being gained or lost.

The same principle applies in a comprehensive dental evaluation. The scan gives the clinician a digital record that can be examined, rotated, enlarged, and reviewed. It helps reveal wear, asymmetry, spacing, restorative limitations, and opportunities for improvement. Critically, it also helps the patient see what the dentist sees.

Patients often struggle to understand dental problems described only in clinical terms. A digital scan changes the conversation. The patient sees the problem. The dentist shows the condition. Specialists can be consulted for additional input. Visual communication creates a more informed patient and a more productive consultation.

SMILE DESIGN AND DIAGNOSTIC WAX-UP

The patient’s records—photography, facial analysis, occlusal evaluation, and digital scan—were combined to create a complete understanding of her aesthetic and functional needs. The goal was to design restorations that improved tooth proportion, color, symmetry, and overall harmony while maintaining a natural appearance.

The digital scan provided the foundation for a diagnostic wax-up (exocad) (Figure 15). This is a critical step in aesthetic dentistry. The wax-up serves as the blueprint for the case, allowing the dentist, laboratory, and patient to evaluate proposed changes before definitive treatment begins. Tooth length, incisal edge position, facial contours, emergence profile, midline, smile curve, and overall proportion can all be refined. Without this step, aesthetic dentistry becomes guesswork. With it, treatment becomes controlled, visual, and predictable.

In racing, you do not show up on race day without a setup.

The car has been tested, the suspension adjusted, the tire pressures selected, and the aerodynamics tuned. The team has a strategy before the lights go out. A diagnostic wax-up serves the same role—it gives the team a visual strategy before treatment begins.

The scan transferred the existing dentition into the digital planning environment, allowing the laboratory to design the proposed smile from a detailed digital record. AI-enhanced smile design tools further accelerated this process by using scan data and patient photographs to generate realistic smile simulations and 3D renderings. The scan is not just a file. It is the starting point for the design.

WHITENING AND PRE-RESTORATIVE COLOR CONTROL

Before final restorative treatment, whitening trays were fabricated from the digital scan, allowing the patient to improve underlying tooth color before definitive restorations were completed. When natural teeth remain visible in the final smile, improving shade before selecting restorative materials helps create a more harmonious outcome. Opalescence by Ultradent was used for whitening.

Using the scan to fabricate whitening trays streamlined the workflow and eliminated the need for an additional impression (Figure 16). The digital record was already captured and could support another phase of treatment. This is one of the key advantages of a modern scanning workflow: one scan serves multiple purposes. In racing, teams engineer out unnecessary weight and friction to go faster. Modern digital workflows do the same—they remove friction.

RESTORATIVE TREATMENT PLAN

After reviewing the diagnostic wax-up, smile design, photographs, scan, and clinical findings, I developed a veneer-based restorative plan guided by each tooth’s condition, structural needs, functional demands, and desired aesthetic outcome.

Each tooth was evaluated individually based on existing dentistry, structural compromise, wear, position, and final color goals. The digital workflow helped guide preparation design, restorative thickness, material selection, occlusion, and laboratory communication, allowing the case to be planned with greater intention before preparation began.

On the racetrack, every decision influences the next. Braking too late affects corner entry. Missing the apex affects exit speed. Poor exit speed costs time on the next straight. Dentistry works the same way. Poor diagnosis affects planning. Poor planning affects preparation. A poor scan affects the laboratory. Poor communication affects fit, form, function, and aesthetics. Performance requires connection.

PREPARATION, SCANNING, AND PROVISIONALIZATION

At the preparation appointment, the diagnostic wax-up guided the clinical workflow. Preparation guides, Beadline provisional stent (Figure 17), and provisional techniques helped control reduction and preserve tooth structure. Tissue management, moisture control, margin visibility, and preparation refinement were essential for an accurate final scan. Additional information on the Beadline technique can be found at the website legiondentist.com/beadline.

After the minimal-preparation, no-preparation veneers were completed, the Ori scanner captured the teeth, the opposing arch, and the bite relationship. The scan was reviewed immediately to verify margin clarity, complete data capture, and occlusal accuracy.

This immediate verification is one of the major advantages of intraoral scanning. With traditional impressions, errors such as voids, distortion, unclear margins, or incomplete data may not be discovered until the laboratory begins working, often leading to delays, remakes, or additional appointments. With a digital workflow, many issues can be identified and corrected chairside before the patient leaves.

In racing, telemetry allows the team to make better decisions sooner. They do not wait until the race is over to discover a problem. They see the data. They respond. They adjust. Digital scanning gives the restorative team a similar advantage.

The final scan, photographs, shade information, preparation details, and clinical notes were sent to the laboratory (Dental Lab Miami) along with the approved smile design and diagnostic wax-up records.

Provisional restorations can be created from the diagnostic wax-up using the Beadline technique, similar to the original mockup used for depth cuts. In this case, however, we chose lab-printed temporary veneers luted with ClearTemp LC Temporary Veneer Cement (Ultradent) to replicate the exact shape designed by the laboratory.

The provisionals allowed the patient and dentist to evaluate the proposed smile—its aesthetics, phonetics, tooth length, lip support, occlusion, and overall satisfaction—before final fabrication. In aesthetic dentistry, provisionals are not merely temporary restorations. They are the test drive.

FINAL DELIVERY

The veneer restorations (IPS e.max [Ivoclar]) were pre-silanated, tried in, and evaluated for marginal fit, proximal contacts, occlusion, color, contour, surface texture, and overall smile harmony using Choice 2 Clear Try-In Paste (BISCO). Here you can see half of the no-prep veneer restorations in place (Figure 18). The result was compared to the diagnostic wax-up, approved provisionals, original smile design, and initial records. Once approved, the restorations were steam cleaned.

The teeth were cleaned with OptiClean (Kerr), etched with Uni-Etch w/BAC (BISCO), and treated with All-Bond Universal (BISCO). The veneers were treated with Porcelain Bonding Resin (BISCO), seated with Choice 2 Translucent Veneer Cement (BISCO), and cured with VALO X (Ultradent). All steps were performed according to manufacturer recommendations.

The final result demonstrated how a digital workflow connects the entire aesthetic process—from comprehensive evaluation through smile design, whitening, preparation, scanning, laboratory communication, and delivery (Figure 19). The scanner was not used at just one point. It became the digital foundation for the entire treatment sequence.

DISCUSSION

Technology does not replace clinical skill. It amplifies it. A scanner does not diagnose. AI does not replace judgment. Smile design software does not create artistry on its own. But when these tools are placed inside a clear system, they can improve diagnosis, communication, efficiency, and the overall patient experience.

In traditional workflows, many steps are disconnected. The exam, photographs, impressions, laboratory communication, treatment planning, and final delivery often function as separate events. Each gap creates drag. Digital scanning and AI help connect those steps into a more efficient and predictable workflow.

In racing, better data allows better decisions. Better decisions create better lines. Better lines create better lap times. Dentistry works the same way. Better data supports better diagnosis, which leads to better treatment planning, better patient communication, better case acceptance, and better restorative delivery.

But technology alone does not create performance. Installing a scanner without a strategy, a trained team, a repeatable workflow, and a clear clinical purpose can leave an expensive piece of equipment underutilized and disconnected from the patient experience. The win comes from the system.

This is one of the principles I teach through the online training program LEGION: technology is only as powerful as the strategy and systems surrounding it. A scanner, AI platform, digital workflow, or restorative material will never realize its full value unless the practice defines how it will be used, who is responsible, how the patient will experience it, and how it connects to diagnosis, communication, treatment planning, and delivery.

Modern dentistry is not suffering from a lack of technology. In many cases, it suffers from a lack of implementation. When scanning, AI, photography, smile design, laboratory collaboration, and restorative dentistry work together as one cohesive performance system, technology becomes more than equipment. It becomes part of how the practice communicates value, increases efficiency, reduces friction, and delivers better care.

That is where speed becomes valuable—not speed for the sake of speed, but speed created by clarity, preparation, and execution. Strategy and systems win the race.

CONCLUSION

The future of dentistry is not slower, more complicated, or more analog. It is faster, smarter, more visual, more efficient, and more connected. Intraoral scanning and artificial intelligence are playing pivotal roles in that transformation—not as isolated tools, but as integrated systems that support clinical care from diagnosis through delivery.

In a modern dental practice, the scan becomes the digital foundation of the case. It helps the dentist and team capture better information, communicate more clearly, reduce friction, and create a more predictable clinical experience.

But technology alone is not enough. The dentist still has to drive.

As in racing, performance comes from the combination of machine, data, skill, precision, strategy, and execution. The fastest car does not win simply because it is fast. It wins because it is engineered, prepared, and driven with purpose. Intraoral scanning and AI can help transform a practice, but only when implemented intentionally and integrated into the entire clinical workflow.

When those elements come together, the result is not just speed. It is control. It is confidence. It is a better patient experience, a stronger practice, and a workflow built to win.

For progressive dental practices, the race toward the next generation of dentistry has already begun. The only question is whether your practice is built to compete.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Dr. Snyder graduated from the UCLA School of Dentistry and the F.A.C.E. Institute. While at UCLA, he co-created and co-directed the first-ever 2-year graduate program in aesthetic and cosmetic dentistry. Dr. Snyder is the 77th Accredited Fellow of the American Academy of Cosmetic Dentistry, a Fellow of the American Society for Dental Aesthetics, a Diplomate of the American Board of Aesthetic Dentistry, and a Fellow of the International Academy of Dental-Facial Esthetics. An internationally recognized author, lecturer, and dental-industry consultant, Dr. Snyder is also the founder of LEGION, a live and online dental education and business training platform. He hosts the weekly podcast, Delusional: Winning the Weekly War of Dentistry. Beyond dentistry, Dr. Snyder is an entrepreneur and professional race car driver. He practices cosmetic and restorative dentistry in Laguna Niguel, Calif, and Las Vegas. Learn more at legiondentist.com or contact Dr. Snyder at legiondentist.com/contact-us.
